imageInfo.caption: Jean de Joinville, kneeling, presents his Life of Saint Louis to the future Louis X in a French manuscript miniature of about 1330–1340.
imageInfo.creator: Attributed to Mahiet, Parisian illuminator
imageInfo.source: Wikimedia Commons (Gallica, Bibliothèque nationale de France), public domain
imageInfo.note: Opening miniature of the oldest surviving copy of Joinville's Life of Saint Louis, the so-called Brussels manuscript, now Bibliothèque nationale de France, français 13568, fol. 1. It shows the presentation of the book in 1309 to Louis, then king of Navarre and count of Champagne, who became Louis X in 1314. The kneeling author wears blue with gold horse-bits, the arms of the lords of Joinville. The copy was made some fifteen to twenty years after Joinville died in 1317, so the figure is a conventional portrait, not a likeness. The attribution to Mahiet follows Commons.

overview: Jean de Joinville was a nobleman and chronicler whose Life of Saint Louis preserves one of the most important accounts of Louis IX and the Seventh Crusade.
His legacy is documentary: he gives the crusades a human voice, attentive to fear, loyalty, piety, and political judgment.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Jean de Joinville was a nobleman and chronicler whose Life of Saint Louis preserves one of the most important accounts of Louis IX and the Seventh Crusade.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Joinville was born into the aristocracy of Champagne and served Louis IX in the eastern expedition to Egypt and the Levant.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Jean de Joinville is remembered through the warm, vivid, and deeply personal memoir he wrote of his friend and king Louis IX, one of the most engaging works of medieval literature, and his own character shines through every page of it. He presents himself as a loyal but independent-minded noble — devoted to the king yet willing to disagree with him, frank about his own fears in battle, his reluctance to join the second crusade, and his attachment to his lands and people.

His personality, as it emerges from his writing, is candid, humane, observant, and touched with humour: he records his own anxieties and comforts as honestly as the king's holiness, and his refusal to swear he would not abandon Louis if the king persisted in a course he thought unwise reveals a man of conscience and plain speaking. His affection for Louis is genuine but never blind.

Because we know him chiefly through his own self-portrait, the picture is shaped by his telling, but its candour and self-deprecation give it credibility. He is remembered as the devoted, honest, and warmly human chronicler of Saint Louis — a noble whose own engaging personality, preserved in his memoir, makes him one of the most likeable individuals to leave a voice from the thirteenth century.

contentSections.title: As chronicler of Saint Louis
paragraphs: Joinville experienced the Seventh Crusade firsthand, including the Egyptian campaign and captivity. His later writing combined memory, moral portrait, eyewitness detail, and royal sanctity.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Joinville died in 1317 after a long life that extended well beyond Louis IX’s canonization.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: His legacy is documentary: he gives the crusades a human voice, attentive to fear, loyalty, piety, and political judgment.
